screens.title: Amazon EventBridge: Building Event Buses
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we explore Amazon EventBridge as a serverless event bus that connects applications, AWS services, and partner SaaS systems. You will learn what an event bus is, how rules use event patterns to filter JSON payloads, and how targets receive events in parallel. We explain how EventBridge differs from a simple publish/subscribe service and why content-based routing matters when you need precise delivery instead of broad broadcast. You will see concrete examples: sending custom events with the PutEvents A P I, writing an event pattern that filters orders by total amount, and connecting a target such as an SQS queue or a Lambda function. We'll also surface common pitfalls — miswritten event patterns and missing permissions — and show safe practices like least-privilege roles and precise JSON matching. By the end you should be able to decide when EventBridge is the right fit, author a rule that matches only the events you want, and attach appropriate targets for event-driven workflows. Consider how content-based routing can reduce downstream processing and limit exposure of sensitive data; that core insight will guide the lab and examples that follow.

Amazon EventBridge: Building Event Buses

Use EventBridge to route structured JSON events from AWS services, your applications, or SaaS partners to targets such as Lambda, SQS, SNS, and Step Functions. Focus on precision: rules match event patterns and route matching events in parallel to multiple targets.

Event Bus
A pipeline that receives events. Every account has a default event bus; you can add custom buses.
Rule
Evaluates events with an event pattern and routes matches to one or more targets.
Target
Any supported AWS resource or another event bus invoked when an event matches a rule.
Explore Key Topics
Routing & Patterns
Build event patterns that match only the payload values you care about.
Sources
AWS services, custom apps via PutEvents, and SaaS partners supply events to buses.
Targets
Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions, Kinesis, and more receive matched events in parallel.
Event Bus Visual
Cards show sources, a bus, rules, and parallel targets to illustrate flow.
Sources
AWS services • Custom apps • SaaS partners
Event Bus
Default or custom buses collect incoming events for rules to evaluate.
Rules & Targets
Rules filter by event pattern and route matched events to targets in parallel.

screens.title: What is an Event Bus and an Event?
screens.narratorSegment: An event bus is a pipeline that receives events and makes them available to rules for routing. Think of the bus as a message highway: many producers put events onto the bus, and rules are the toll booths that decide who receives each event. An event itself is a structured JSON object describing a change or occurrence — for example, an order placed event contains fields such as orderId, totalAmount, and status. Events from AWS services flow automatically into the default event bus; custom applications and SaaS partners can send events to either the default or a custom bus. Understanding the distinction matters because custom buses let you separate domains, apply different access rules, and reduce accidental routing between systems. A common misconception is that an event bus stores events; it does not act as durable storage by default. Instead, it routes events to targets that may persist or process them. A concrete example: an order microservice calls PutEvents with a detailType of OrderService. OrderPlaced and a detail payload that includes totalAmount. A rule on the bus can then inspect totalAmount and route only high-value orders to a high-value processing Lambda. Key takeaway: design your buses and event formats to make rules simple and precise, which reduces downstream complexity and permissions scope.

keyIdea.title: Event vs Bus
keyIdea.text: The event bus receives JSON events; events are payloads that describe changes and are evaluated by rules for routing.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Event Bus & Event
Definition
Event Bus

A pipeline receiving events from AWS services, custom apps, or SaaS integrations. Default and custom buses let you control routing domains.

Definition
Event (JSON)

A JSON object carrying details about a change. Fields such as source, detail-type, and detail are used by rules to match content.

Example Event (excerpt)
{
  "Source": "com.mycompany.myapp",
  "DetailType": "OrderService.OrderPlaced",
  "Detail": "{ \"orderId\": \"ORD-XYZ-789\", \"totalAmount\": 150.75 }",
  "EventBusName": "default"
}
Why it matters
Clear event formats and separated buses make writing precise event patterns easier and reduce accidental delivery. Separate buses for domains help isolate permissions and auditing.
Key Takeaway

Design events with consistent keys and types so rules can match values without complex transformations.

Common Mistake
Treating the event bus as durable storage. Use targets like SQS, Kinesis, or databases for persistence.

screens.title: Rules, Event Patterns, and Targets
screens.narratorSegment: Rules are the heart of EventBridge: a rule evaluates incoming events against an event pattern and, when a match occurs, routes the event to its targets. An event pattern is a JSON structure that inspects keys and values inside the event. Patterns support exact matches and advanced operators such as numeric comparisons. Importantly, a single rule can have multiple targets and all targets are invoked in parallel. This parallel model is powerful but has implications: each target must be prepared to process the original event shape. For example, you might have a rule that routes OrderPlaced events to a payment service only when totalAmount exceeds a threshold and also sends every order to a fraud service, or you might route large orders to a special queue for manual review. A frequent pitfall is writing a pattern that is too broad, which routes unnecessary events, or too narrow, which drops valid events. Another common issue is forgetting to grant EventBridge permission to invoke the target: Lambda needs lambda:InvokeFunction, SQS may need queue policy adjustments, and other targets require their own permissions. The practical rule-of-thumb is to design event patterns to be as tight as possible and to provision least-privilege roles so that EventBridge can only invoke the intended targets.

keyIdea.title: Rules in Parallel
keyIdea.text: A rule filters events using an event pattern and can invoke multiple targets in parallel, so design patterns and permissions carefully.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Rules & Targets
How Rules Work
A rule evaluates every incoming event on the bus. If the event pattern matches, the rule sends the event to all configured targets in parallel.
Event Pattern Example
Match OrderService.OrderPlaced events where totalAmount is greater than a threshold.
{
  "source": ["com.mycompany.myapp"],
  "detail-type": ["OrderService.OrderPlaced"],
  "detail": { "totalAmount": [{"numeric": [">", 100]}] }
}
Targets in Parallel
  • Lambda functions for compute and business logic.
  • SQS for durable buffering and retries.
  • Step Functions for orchestrated workflows.
  • SNS, Kinesis, other EventBridge buses as needed.
Common Mistake
Writing event patterns that don't match due to incorrect key names or data types. Validate patterns with test events.
Key Takeaway

Use precise patterns and grant minimal invoke permissions to targets so matching is reliable and secure.

screens.title: EventBridge vs SNS
screens.narratorSegment: EventBridge and SNS are both useful for event-driven designs, but they serve different primary problems. SNS is a publish/subscribe messaging service optimized for fan-out: a single published message is delivered to all subscribers regardless of its content. It's simple and effective when you want broad distribution, such as sending the same notification to email, SMS, and queues. EventBridge, by contrast, is a content-based event router. It examines the structure and values inside a JSON event and routes only matching events to targets. Use EventBridge when different consumers need to react to specific events or values, for example routing high-value orders to a specialized processor while still sending every order to an audit trail. A common misconception is to use EventBridge when SNS would suffice; this can overcomplicate simple broadcast cases. Conversely, SNS cannot match nested JSON fields the way EventBridge patterns can, so using SNS for payload-based routing forces extra filtering downstream. The practical guidance: choose SNS for simple broadcasting, choose EventBridge when your architecture relies on filtering by the event's content and you want tight, declarative routing in the event plane.

keyIdea.title: When to Use Which
keyIdea.text: SNS for simple fan-out broadcasts; EventBridge for content-based routing and filtering of structured JSON events.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › EventBridge vs SNS
SNS — Fan-out
Publish a message once and deliver it to multiple subscribers without inspecting the message content. Good for notifications and broad distribution.
Use when
  • You need simple broadcast to many endpoints.
  • No need to examine payload fields to decide delivery.
EventBridge — Content-based Routing
Inspect event JSON and route only matching events to targets. Support for structured filters and numeric operators makes it ideal for complex routing rules.
Use when
  • Different consumers react to different event types or values.
  • You need declarative routing based on event content.
Concrete Example
For a billing system, use SNS to broadcast billing updates to monitoring, billing reports, and a marketing subscription. Use EventBridge to route OrderPlaced events with totalAmount over a threshold to a high-value order processor while routing all orders to an audit queue.

screens.title: Putting Custom Events with Boto3
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the Python example that demonstrates the common workflow: put a custom event, prepare an SQS target, create a rule with an event pattern, and attach the SQS ARN as a target. The code initializes an EventBridge client and builds a custom event object with a source, a detail type, and a detail payload serialized as JSON. The code calls PutEvents with that entry to publish to the default bus. Next, the snippet creates or retrieves an SQS queue and extracts its ARN; you then create an EventBridge rule that contains an event pattern matching the source and a numeric condition for totalAmount. Finally, add the SQS queue as a target to the rule. In practice you'll also need to ensure EventBridge has permission to send to the SQS queue — typically via an IAM role or a permissive queue policy. This example is practical: run it to observe a matching message arriving in SQS when the totalAmount is above the threshold and no message when it is below. Remember, do not treat the code as production-ready without adding error handling and least-privilege IAM roles, but it captures the essential A P I calls and ordering you need to implement.

keyIdea.title: PutEvents Workflow
keyIdea.text: Use PutEvents to publish custom JSON events, then create rules and attach targets such as SQS; validate with test events.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › PutEvents Example
Code Excerpt (Python / Boto3)
import boto3
import json

# Initialize EventBridge client
events = boto3.client('events', region_name='us-east-1')

custom_event = {
  'Source': 'com.mycompany.myapp',
  'DetailType': 'OrderService.OrderPlaced',
  'Detail': json.dumps({
    'orderId': 'ORD-XYZ-789',
    'customerId': 'C-456',
    'totalAmount': 150.75,
    'status': 'PENDING'
  }),
  'EventBusName': 'default'
}

response = events.put_events(Entries=[custom_event])
print('Custom event put to EventBridge:', response)
Sequence
  1. Publish a custom event with PutEvents.
  2. Create or ensure an SQS queue exists and get its ARN.
  3. Create a rule with an event pattern matching the event.
  4. Add the SQS queue as a target to the rule and verify permissions.
Practical Tip
Test with two events: one below the numeric threshold and one above, to confirm that only matching events reach the target.
Key Takeaway

The PutEvents + rule + target pattern is the standard way to inject custom events and route them declaratively.

Step 1
Create a Python 3.9 Lambda named HighValueOrderProcessor with CloudWatch logging. Ensure the role allows basic logging.
Step 2
Create an EventBridge rule HighValueOrderRule on the default bus with an event pattern filtering your source, detail-type, and totalAmount numeric condition greater than threshold.

screens.title: Sources and Targets: Practical Integrations
screens.narratorSegment: EventBridge supports three broad source types: AWS services, custom applications, and SaaS partner integrations. AWS services such as S3, EC2, and DynamoDB can emit events into the default bus automatically, giving you a stream of resource state changes. Custom applications use the PutEvents A P I to send events with a source and detail type that you control. SaaS partners can be configured to send events directly into EventBridge as well. On the target side, EventBridge integrates with Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions, Kinesis, EC2, and other event buses. This breadth lets you choose synchronous compute, durable queues, orchestration, or data streams as the right consumer. When designing an architecture, think about whether the target needs durability, retry semantics, or orchestration. For example, send events that require retries or batching to SQS, orchestrated workflows to Step Functions, and immediate processing to Lambda. Also consider that targets run in parallel, so ensure idempotency in downstream processors where duplicates or simultaneous invocations could cause issues. The practical significance is that EventBridge is the glue: it receives diverse inputs and reliably fans out to the set of targets best suited to handle the event semantics.

keyIdea.title: Integration Glue
keyIdea.text: EventBridge unifies AWS, custom, and SaaS sources and delivers events to many types of targets, letting you choose the right consumer for each event type.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Sources & Targets
Event Sources
  • AWS Services: Over 200 services can emit events to the default bus.
  • Custom Apps: Use PutEvents to publish structured JSON events.
  • SaaS Partners: Third-party systems can send events directly to EventBridge.
Event Targets
  • Lambda for immediate processing.
  • SQS for durable buffering and retry decoupling.
  • Step Functions for orchestrated workflows.
  • Kinesis or other buses for streaming and cross-account routing.
Design Guidance
Choose targets based on durability and processing guarantees. Use SQS for retries and dead-letter handling, Lambda for compute, and Step Functions for longer-running orchestrations. Ensure downstream idempotency when parallel invocations are possible.

screens.title: Permissions and Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Two permission-related pitfalls commonly break EventBridge integrations. First, EventBridge must have permission to invoke its targets. For Lambda, EventBridge needs a resource-based policy that allows lambda:InvokeFunction from the EventBus or the rule's principal. For SQS, ensure the queue policy permits events to send messages or attach an IAM role that allows EventBridge to send to the queue. The second pitfall is misconfiguring event patterns: patterns are strict about keys and data types, so using the wrong key name or expecting a number where the event contains a string will cause mismatches. screens.title: Testing and Validation Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable testing flow makes it easy to validate that your EventBridge rule and targets behave as expected. Start with a staging or test bus to avoid affecting production. Step one: author the event pattern and save the rule in a paused or guarded state to prevent accidental traffic. Step two: send controlled test events using PutEvents — send one event designed to match and another designed not to match. Step three: observe the target: for Lambda check CloudWatch logs, for SQS inspect messages, and for Step Functions check executions. Step four: verify permissions by simulating invocation and reading any error messages that indicate missing invoke permissions. Finally, iterate: adjust the pattern and repeat tests until only the intended events match. Using this timeline reduces errors and prevents noisy production behavior. A common misconception is that one successful test proves correctness; instead, test a variety of payload shapes, nested keys, and edge-case numeric boundaries to ensure robust matching. This validation strategy gives confidence when you flip the rule fully into production. In this chapter we explore Amazon EventBridge as a serverless event bus that connects applications, AWS services, and partner SaaS systems. You will learn what an event bus is, how rules use event patterns to filter JSON payloads, and how targets receive events in parallel. We explain how EventBridge differs from a simple publish/subscribe service and why content-based routing matters when you need precise delivery instead of broad broadcast. You will see concrete examples: sending custom events with the PutEvents A P I, writing an event pattern that filters orders by total amount, and connecting a target such as an SQS queue or a Lambda function. We'll also surface common pitfalls — miswritten event patterns and missing permissions — and show safe practices like least-privilege roles and precise JSON matching. By the end you should be able to decide when EventBridge is the right fit, author a rule that matches only the events you want, and attach appropriate targets for event-driven workflows. Consider how content-based routing can reduce downstream processing and limit exposure of sensitive data; that core insight will guide the lab and examples that follow.

These objectives prepare you to design event-driven solutions with EventBridge. First, you will explain EventBridge as a serverless event bus — what it receives and how it routes events — so you can choose the right service for event-driven needs. Second, you will be able to contrast EventBridge with SNS, recognizing that SNS is a fan-out messaging service while EventBridge is a content-based router; that distinction is essential when deciding whether to broadcast or filter by payload contents. Third, you'll author rules with event patterns to filter events: you will write JSON patterns that match specific keys and numeric conditions so services only process relevant events. Fourth, you will integrate sources and targets: you will send custom events with PutEvents and attach Lambda, SQS, or other AWS targets, ensuring EventBridge has the proper permissions. Each objective focuses on applied skills: diagnosing when to use EventBridge, implementing precise filters, and safely wiring targets. By mastering these objectives you'll reduce unnecessary processing, protect sensitive data, and build more maintainable, loosely coupled architectures.

This objective screen connects each skill to a practical check you can perform. For explaining EventBridge, demonstrate that you can identify a default bus versus a custom bus and describe events as JSON payloads that represent state changes. For differentiating EventBridge and SNS, show a decision: choose SNS when you need to broadcast a message to many subscribers without inspecting content, and choose EventBridge when routing must inspect fields inside the JSON payload. For authoring event patterns, write and test a pattern that matches an order event only when a numeric field exceeds a threshold; verify with two test events: one that does not match and one that does. For integrating sources and targets, produce a short workflow that sends a custom event with PutEvents and proves a Lambda or SQS target received the matching message. Each micro-task maps to a verified competency milestone so you can self-check. These checks are practical and repeatable, ensuring you don't just know the definitions but can actually implement and validate them.

An event bus is a pipeline that receives events and makes them available to rules for routing. Think of the bus as a message highway: many producers put events onto the bus, and rules are the toll booths that decide who receives each event. An event itself is a structured JSON object describing a change or occurrence — for example, an order placed event contains fields such as orderId, totalAmount, and status. Events from AWS services flow automatically into the default event bus; custom applications and SaaS partners can send events to either the default or a custom bus. Understanding the distinction matters because custom buses let you separate domains, apply different access rules, and reduce accidental routing between systems. A common misconception is that an event bus stores events; it does not act as durable storage by default. Instead, it routes events to targets that may persist or process them. A concrete example: an order microservice calls PutEvents with a detailType of OrderService. OrderPlaced and a detail payload that includes totalAmount. A rule on the bus can then inspect totalAmount and route only high-value orders to a high-value processing Lambda. Key takeaway: design your buses and event formats to make rules simple and precise, which reduces downstream complexity and permissions scope.

Rules are the heart of EventBridge: a rule evaluates incoming events against an event pattern and, when a match occurs, routes the event to its targets. An event pattern is a JSON structure that inspects keys and values inside the event. Patterns support exact matches and advanced operators such as numeric comparisons. Importantly, a single rule can have multiple targets and all targets are invoked in parallel. This parallel model is powerful but has implications: each target must be prepared to process the original event shape. For example, you might have a rule that routes OrderPlaced events to a payment service only when totalAmount exceeds a threshold and also sends every order to a fraud service, or you might route large orders to a special queue for manual review. A frequent pitfall is writing a pattern that is too broad, which routes unnecessary events, or too narrow, which drops valid events. Another common issue is forgetting to grant EventBridge permission to invoke the target: Lambda needs lambda:InvokeFunction, SQS may need queue policy adjustments, and other targets require their own permissions. The practical rule-of-thumb is to design event patterns to be as tight as possible and to provision least-privilege roles so that EventBridge can only invoke the intended targets.

EventBridge and SNS are both useful for event-driven designs, but they serve different primary problems. SNS is a publish/subscribe messaging service optimized for fan-out: a single published message is delivered to all subscribers regardless of its content. It's simple and effective when you want broad distribution, such as sending the same notification to email, SMS, and queues. EventBridge, by contrast, is a content-based event router. It examines the structure and values inside a JSON event and routes only matching events to targets. Use EventBridge when different consumers need to react to specific events or values, for example routing high-value orders to a specialized processor while still sending every order to an audit trail. A common misconception is to use EventBridge when SNS would suffice; this can overcomplicate simple broadcast cases. Conversely, SNS cannot match nested JSON fields the way EventBridge patterns can, so using SNS for payload-based routing forces extra filtering downstream. The practical guidance: choose SNS for simple broadcasting, choose EventBridge when your architecture relies on filtering by the event's content and you want tight, declarative routing in the event plane.

Let's walk through the Python example that demonstrates the common workflow: put a custom event, prepare an SQS target, create a rule with an event pattern, and attach the SQS ARN as a target. The code initializes an EventBridge client and builds a custom event object with a source, a detail type, and a detail payload serialized as JSON. The code calls PutEvents with that entry to publish to the default bus. Next, the snippet creates or retrieves an SQS queue and extracts its ARN; you then create an EventBridge rule that contains an event pattern matching the source and a numeric condition for totalAmount. Finally, add the SQS queue as a target to the rule. In practice you'll also need to ensure EventBridge has permission to send to the SQS queue — typically via an IAM role or a permissive queue policy. This example is practical: run it to observe a matching message arriving in SQS when the totalAmount is above the threshold and no message when it is below. Remember, do not treat the code as production-ready without adding error handling and least-privilege IAM roles, but it captures the essential A P I calls and ordering you need to implement.
